faq: How long does a project take?
A landing page usually takes 3–7 days. A full website or app takes 2–4 weeks, depending on the number of screens.
What do I need to get started?
Just your idea, your goals and any brand materials you have. If you don't have a brand yet, I can create one.
Do you also build the website?
I focus on design and deliver clean Figma files ready for developers. I can also build on Webflow or Framer when needed.
How many revisions do I get?
Every project includes revision rounds, so you are happy with the final result.
You can hire me through Fiverr or directly. Direct projects usually start with a 50% deposit.

metrics.label: Checkout
metrics.cap: fewer steps to place an order

steps.title: Challenge
body: A growing food delivery service with 20K+ monthly users wanted its app to feel faster and friendlier, but the path to checkout was long and confusing.
Many carts were left before payment, search results were hard to scan and delivery fees appeared only at the last step.

steps.title: Process
body: I ran 12 user interviews, audited 5 competitor apps and reviewed 200+ support tickets, then set one goal: get from hunger to order in under a minute.
Wireframes and a clickable prototype were tested with 15 people over 3 rounds. The final UI uses a warm palette, large food photography and a reusable Figma component library.

steps.title: Result
body: Checkout now takes 35% fewer steps, a past order can be repeated in two taps and the team has 40+ reusable components to build new features faster.
Next steps: personalised recommendations, group ordering and dark mode.

5-ui-mistakes-that-make-users-leave-your.sum: Small design problems that quietly push people away — and simple ways to fix them.
body: Most people don't delete an app because of one big problem. They leave because of many small moments that feel slow, confusing or annoying. After designing apps for fintech, fitness and food delivery clients, I keep seeing the same mistakes.
Here are five of them, and what I do instead.

body.h2: 1. Asking for too much, too early

body: Long sign-up forms before the user sees any value are the fastest way to lose them. Let people explore first, and ask for details only when they are needed.

body.h2: 2. Buttons that don't look like buttons

body: Flat text links, low-contrast colours and tiny tap areas make users guess. Every main action should be obvious at first glance and easy to tap with one thumb.

body.quote: If a user has to think about where to tap, the design has already failed.

body: Showing fees or limits only at the last step breaks trust. Be honest early — a clear total on the first screen converts better than a surprise at checkout.
When a user taps and nothing happens, they tap again, or leave. Every action needs a response: a loading state, a success message or a clear error.

list: Show a loading state for anything over half a second
Confirm success with a short message or animation
Write errors in plain words and say how to fix them
Never lose what the user already typed

body.h2: 5. Too many things on one screen

body: Trying to show everything at once makes nothing stand out. Pick one main goal per screen and move the rest one tap away.
Fixing these five problems doesn't need a full redesign. Small, focused changes can make an app feel faster, clearer and more trustworthy — and that is what keeps people coming back.

how-i-design-a-landing-page-that-convert.sum: My step-by-step process for landing pages that turn visitors into leads.
body: A landing page has one job: get the visitor to take one action. Everything on the page should help with that job, or it should go.

body.h2: Start with the message, not the layout

body: Before I open Figma, I write the headline, the main benefit and the call to action. If those three are not clear in words, no design will save the page.

body.quote: Visitors decide in a few seconds whether to stay. The headline has to do the work.

body.h2: Answer three questions at the top

body: If the first screen answers these three questions, most of the work is done.
Below the hero I add proof: results, client logos, reviews and examples. Then I answer common doubts in a short FAQ, and repeat the call to action at the end.
A clear message, a simple structure and honest proof — that is what turns a nice-looking page into one that actually brings in leads.

what-i-learned-from-my-first-50-fiverr-o.sum: Lessons on clients, communication and pricing from my early freelance work.
body: My first Fiverr orders taught me more about running a design business than any course. Here is what I wish I had known on day one.

body.h2: Communication matters as much as design

body: Clients remember how the project felt. Quick replies, clear updates and honest timelines build trust even before they see the first design.

body.h2: Ask more questions before you start

body: Most revision rounds come from a weak brief. Now I always ask about goals, audience, examples they like and what success looks like.

body.quote: A good brief saves more time than a fast designer.

body.h2: What I do on every order now

list: Send a short summary of the brief before starting
Share early wireframes, not just final designs
Agree on the number of revisions up front

body: Happier clients, fewer revisions and more repeat orders. Good process turned one-time buyers into long-term clients.
